assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model predicted flat bands at a magic twist angle, and the 2018 observations of correlated insulators and superconductivity opened twistronics, a new platform for strongly correlated electrons with tunable parameters. From a first-principles and many-body perspective it is both conceptually clean and remarkably original, and it has spawned a large field (moire materials, fractional Chern insulators).
assessment.attribution: A theory-prediction plus experimental-discovery configuration fits three names well: Bistritzer and MacDonald for the prediction, Jarillo-Herrero for the experimental realization. Other groups (for example Cao as first author, Dean and Young on related moire work, and earlier twisted-bilayer theory by Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto) have claims that the credited list cannot fully capture.
assessment.maturity: Independently reproduced by many groups; the interpretation of the superconducting mechanism remains unsettled, but the flat-band and correlated-insulator phenomenology is well established. Recognition is timely and arguably the most compelling of the recent condensed-matter discoveries.
uncertainties: Pairing mechanism of superconductivity in twisted graphene is still debated.
Priority questions around earlier twisted-bilayer band-structure theory and the choice of experimental credit.
Whether the moire family (WSe2, fractional Chern insulators) should be folded into this recognition.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, using the magic-wavelength idea to trap neutral atoms without perturbing the clock transition, reached fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 and underpin tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and a prospective redefinition of the second. The importance, clarity and lasting impact are very high.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and demonstrated the first strontium lattice clock; Ye led the highest-precision realizations and many-body (spin-correlation) clock physics. A two-person prize is natural. Contributions by Takamoto, Ludlow and others sit within these groups, and the NIST/JILA lineage is shared.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by multiple independent laboratories worldwide; the technology is stable and still maturing toward the redefinition of the second, so timing is appropriate.
uncertainties: Prior precision-metrology recognition (frequency combs, 2005) may make the committee cautious about metrology overlap.
Credit sharing with other groups (for example Ye's JILA colleagues and other Sr and Yb clock groups).

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamical mean-field theory is the modern workhorse for treating strongly correlated electrons non-perturbatively, capturing the Mott transition and the coexistence of Hubbard bands and quasiparticles. Combined with density functional theory (DFT+DMFT) it enables material-specific predictions for correlated oxides, f-electron systems and iron-based superconductors, which is directly relevant to how electronic-structure theory is used in practice.
assessment.attribution: Georges and Kotliar built the DMFT mapping onto an impurity problem (1992) and later the DFT+DMFT framework; Vollhardt contributed the infinite-dimension limit work. The foundational infinite-dimension limit is due to Metzner and Vollhardt, and the credited list omits Metzner and Mueller-Hartmann, so allocation is not fully clean. I name three from the supplied list.
assessment.maturity: Mature: four decades of use, validation against spectroscopy and cold-atom simulations. Quantitative accuracy still depends on impurity solvers and the downfolding choices; nonetheless the method is established and widely trusted.
uncertainties: Omitted foundational contributors (Metzner, Mueller-Hartmann) complicate attribution.
Whether a method paper is judged a discovery or an invention for prize purposes.
Material-specific accuracy of DFT+DMFT depends on double-counting and projection choices.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Nd-Fe-B permanent magnet is the strongest commercial permanent magnet and is essential in motors, wind turbines, hard drives and electric vehicles. Its scientific basis is the combination of rare-earth 4f anisotropy and itinerant 3d exchange in Nd2Fe14B, a subject of long electronic-structure and atomistic-modelling interest. The impact on technology and energy transition is very large, though the discovery is materials-engineering in character.
assessment.attribution: Sagawa (Sumitomo) and Croat (General Motors) independently discovered the compound's magnetic usefulness in 1983-84 by different routes, sintered versus melt-spun. Two laureates is a natural fit, though the priority and patent history is contested and Sagawa's contribution is usually seen as primary.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature and confirmed by decades of industrial use, so recognition is long overdue rather than premature. The question is whether the committee considers it physics rather than materials invention.
uncertainties: Disputed priority and patent history between the two credited discoverers.
Fit with the physics-prize remit given that this is an engineered material.
Contributions of the broader rare-earth magnet community (for example Herbst and the Nd2Fe14B structure determinations) are not credited.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Z2 topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect revealed a new class of band insulators characterized by protected edge or surface states, a conceptual shift beyond the 2016 prize on topological phases. It connects directly to spin-orbit physics and spectroscopy that I know well, and it has had very high influence on materials discovery.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the decisive 2005 theory of the Z2 invariant; Molenkamp led the 2007 HgTe observation, which followed the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction (Zhang is deceased and Bernevig is not credited). Hasan's ARPES confirmation of three-dimensional topological insulators is a strong competing claim to the third place. The attribution is therefore contested but supportable with these three.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed by many groups in 2D and 3D; the interpretation is stable. The topological-matter area was recognised in 2016, which raises a question of overlap rather than prematurity.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2016 prize on topological phase transitions.
Absence of Bernevig and Hughes from the credited names and the omission of Zhang.
Whether Hasan or Molenkamp should take the third place.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Reproducible room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance in magnetic tunnel junctions (1995) made spin-dependent tunnelling practical and led to MgO-based read heads and MRAM. Its origin lies in spin-polarized tunnelling and interface electronic structure, an area where first-principles calculations were decisive.
assessment.attribution: Moodera and Miyazaki independently reported the room-temperature effect in 1995; Parkin's contribution is chiefly the large MgO-based TMR and the broader spin-valve engineering, with Yuasa and Djayaprawira (not credited) also central to MgO. This configuration is plausible but allocation is delicate. The 2007 prize (GMR) is a close precedent that reduces novelty.
assessment.maturity: Mature, widely confirmed and industrially deployed; recognition would not be premature, but is partly overshadowed by the GMR prize.
uncertainties: Close relationship to the 2007 GMR prize may be judged incremental.
Omission of Julliere (1975) and the MgO-coherent-tunnelling pioneers from the credited names.
Parkin's contribution is arguably more to MgO TMR and racetrack work than to the 1995 discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Angle-resolved photoemission directly maps electronic band structure, Fermi surfaces, gaps and many-body self-energies, and in the hands of Shen, Campuzano and colleagues it became central to cuprate superconductivity and topological matter. Comparing calculated and measured spectra is a recurring theme in my own field. The lasting impact on quantum materials is high, but the prize question is whether a technique rather than a discovery qualifies.
assessment.attribution: Credit is diffuse: ARPES development spans many groups (Plummer, Johnson, Smith, Hufner and others), and the supplied list gives three. I would restrict to Shen and Campuzano for the cuprate-era breakthroughs, acknowledging that Johnson is also credited but contributions are hard to separate.
assessment.maturity: Highly mature, with extensive independent use; the main uncertainty is conceptual clarity of a single decisive discovery rather than maturity.
uncertainties: A spectroscopy technique with diffuse historical credit may not meet the single-discovery bar.
Missing foundational ARPES developers from the credited names.
Whether the recognition should be tied to cuprates, to topological states or to the instrument.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Altermagnetism identifies a third class of collinear magnetic order with compensated moments yet spin-split bands set by crystal symmetry, with large potential for spintronics. It is conceptually elegant and directly relevant to magnetic-structure theory based on symmetry and first-principles band calculations.
assessment.attribution: The symmetry classification and the unification of earlier observations were articulated by Šmejkal, Sinova and Jungwirth; the three names are consistent with the leading contributors, although related earlier work on spin-split antiferromagnets (Hayami, Yuan, Naka and others) is not credited.
assessment.maturity: Experimental confirmation by ARPES and magnetic circular dichroism in MnTe and CrSb is recent, and technological relevance is unproven. Recognition now looks premature compared with other candidates, hence the lowest place among my eight.
uncertainties: Premature: few years of independent confirmation and incomplete device demonstration.
Priority questions with earlier spin-splitting work in antiferromagnets by Hayami, Yuan and others.
Which material experiments will prove decisive for the interpretation.
